providers.name: Državni arhiv u Pazinu
providers.what: The Pazin State Archive, which holds the parish registers of central Istria. They will search, certify and post a named record for a fee. Its registers are also filmed as the ZM34K series, supplied as page images. Two of those reels were mapped frame by frame on 30 September 2026 and their contents recorded, because the archive's own paper inventory proved unreliable for them: ZM34K-214 and ZM34K-215 together run M01068774-M01070236 (1,463 contiguous frames) and hold THIRTEEN books - Cerovlje status animarum XIX-XX c.; Gologorica baptisms 1764-1788, 1770-1781, 1784-1880 and 1940-1948, deaths 1646-1806 and 1784-1880, marriages 1770-1789, and status animarum for 1826, 1862, 1894 and 1921; and Gracisce baptisms 1667-1745 with confirmations 1690-1694, and baptisms 1746-1840. TWO TRAPS. The paper inventory's section headings file both Gracisce books under a GOLOGORICA heading, and it stops the Gracisce baptisms at 1780 when the film's own title card says 1840. LINDAR IS NOT ON THESE TWO REELS - it is on ZM34K-219 and 220. Each book is preceded by a printed title card naming the zupa, the register and the years; that card, not the inventory, is the authority. WALKED SO FAR, so the next reader need not repeat it: on ZM34K-214 the GOLOGORICA DEATH REGISTER 1784-1880 is read ENTRY BY ENTRY end to end - M01069226-M01069297 (cover, flyleaf and pages 1-135, 96 years), plus its alphabetical INDEX at M01069299-M01069313, with M01069314 the film's own KRAJ / END OF ITEM target. Three things about that book are worth knowing before opening it. (1) Its index is a HOUSEHOLD directory, not a name list: each block is a surname, a byname, a HOUSE NUMBER and then the household's dead with the page each is on - and a married woman is entered under her HUSBAND'S surname, so a name search of the index will miss her. (2) The index ends with a column headed Extranei listing the people who died in the parish and did not belong to it, each with the place they came from - a ready-made list of where this parish's incomers originated, naming Krbune, Cerovlje and Friuli. (3) The index sometimes carries detail the register entry itself omits, so it is a second witness and not only a finding aid. The film also DUPLICATES some openings, and twice the duplicate exposure was the only readable one. Frame numbering of the other twelve books on these reels is in the 30 September mapping above. ALSO WALKED on ZM34K-214: the GOLOGORICA STATUS ANIMARUM of 1826 (M01069315-M01069435), and in particular its printed column 'Locus ex quo vel ad quem' - whence, or whither - read across every opening. That column is the most useful thing on either reel for anyone tracing movement in central Istria: for each household it names the PARISH a person came from or went to, THE HOUSE NUMBER AT THE FAR END, and the year. Counting it out for Gologorica gives Gracisce 16, Paz 9, Novaki 8, Krbune 6, Gradinje 6, Pazin 4, Cerovlje 3, DragUc 3, Lindar 2, Dol 2, Zminj 1, Vrsar 1, Volosca 1, plus 9 moves between houses inside the village itself. Two warnings for whoever reads it next. (1) An opening of this census is ONE table across TWO pages: the left half carries names, rank and birth dates, the right half carries confirmation, marriage, death, the Locus column and vaccination. Reading only the left half loses the origins entirely. (2) The book is ordered by RANK at the front - the 'civilitas' first, then 'rusticus' and 'agricola' - and only settles into house-number order about page 20, and many of the front pages are a HOUSE with an owner named and no household entered under him, because the second column is headed 'Nrus. Inquilinorum' - tenants. A page heading is not a family. ALSO WALKED, and this one is now COMPLETE: on ZM34K-215 the GRACISCE (Gallignana) BAPTISM BOOK 1667-1745, signatura 3.1, is read FRAME BY FRAME end to end - M01069943 to M01070130, 188 frames, title card to the film's KRAJ / END OF ITEM target, every frame, none sampled. Five things the next reader should know before opening it. (1) IT IS TWO REGISTERS, NOT ONE. The title card says MATICNA KNJIGA RODENIH 1667-1745 and MATICNA KNJIGA KRIZMANIH 1690-1694, and the second half is real and substantial: folios 165-171 are a CONFIRMATION ROLL of 16 September 1690 under Bishop Joannes Marcus Rossetti, and folios 174-175 a second of 15 June 1694 under Bishop Petrus Antonius Delle de Hohenberg, numbered to 74. Each line gives child, parent and sponsor. A confirmation roll is the parish's children gathered on ONE DAY before the bishop, so for presence-or-absence questions it is better evidence than a baptism series - and these two are easy to miss because a name-indexed or year-ranged search of 'baptisms 1667-1745' will never reach them. (2) THE BOOK CERTIFIES ITS OWN GAPS. On folio 134 (M01070082), between entries of 17 July and 12 August 1732, the Vicar General Francesco Agostino Corsi - who styles himself on folio 137 'Vic.us Gen.lis Petenensis et Praepositus Pisini', Vicar General of Pedena and Provost of Pazin - left a visitation decree recording that baptisms had been OMITTED from the register through negligence and ordering them recovered and entered without delay. Any nil reported from the baptism half must carry that decree with it. A second visitation mark, 'Revisum in Visitatione &c. die 5. Maij 1745', is drawn across the foot of folio 163 with no complaint attached. (3) IT IS NOT IN CHRONOLOGICAL ORDER, and the decree explains why. Folio 136 carries 1735-1736 while folio 138 carries 1733-1734; at the foot of folio 138 sits a block of six baptisms of April 1732 - January 1733 in a smaller hand under a one-word heading, written in after the fact. A stray baptism of 20 November 1722 sits at the very back, after the confirmation rolls. A SWEEP OF THIS BOOK THAT STEPS BY TWO, OR THAT TRUSTS DATES TO RUN FORWARD, IS NOT A SWEEP. (4) THE FILM'S FRAME COUNT IS NOT THE BOOK'S LEAF COUNT. Three frame-pairs are two exposures of ONE opening, re-shot with a loose slip moved so the text beneath could be read: M01070086/87 (folio 137), M01070093/94 (folio 143), M01070116/117 (folios 164v-165). The second exposure is sometimes the only readable one. (5) THE LAST WRITTEN LEAF IS NOT A REGISTER PAGE. Folio 177 (M01070129) carries the address panel of a folded letter: 'Al Molto Rev.do In Christo Padre ... P. Valeriano da Fiume, Predicatore e Vicario della Venerabile Religione Capucina di Fiume'. A Capuchin letter-cover from Fiume bound into the back of a central-Istrian parish register. Four bishops of Pedena appear in this one volume - von Raunach baptising in person in 1672, Rossetti confirming in 1690, Delle de Hohenberg confirming in 1694, and Josephus Bonifacius Ceccoti baptising in person twice in seven weeks in 1743 - which is worth knowing for a diocese whose own canons swore that no bishop had ever resided in it. Recurring surnames across the whole volume, for anyone deciding whether it is worth their time: Martinich, Milotich, Drusetich, Grach, Baxa, Salamon, Fernasar, Sestan, Poldrugovaz, Dermit, Braissa, Dilizza, Cincopan, Jerbulla, Carlovich, Lupigna, Bertetich, Merletich, Maurovich, Chlaj, Picot, Scuich, Vale, Zotar, Sirol, Lanza, Brosan, Bursich, Copicich, Godenich. NO FAMILYSEARCH WAYPOINT EXISTS for this book: it is a DAPA film, read from a private copy of the reel, not a FamilySearch collection - so it is recorded here by signatura and frame range rather than by a waypoint. ONE MORE THING ABOUT THE GRACISCE BAPTISMS, for anyone who reads them for a surname. From about 1783 (frame M01070190 onward on ZM34K-215) the book stops being narrative Latin and becomes a RULED TABLE, and its columns are: year/month/day, house number, child's name, religion, sex, legitimacy, Pater, Mater, Patrini (Nomen), CONDITIO, Baptizans. Two warnings follow. (1) READING ONE COLUMN IS NOT READING THE BOOK. A sweep of the Pater column of M01070190-M01070226 - about 900 baptisms, 1783 to May 1808 - produced a clean nil for one surname; the PATRINI column of the very same frames then produced about twenty occurrences of it. A surname can sit in Pater, in Mater (written as 'olim' or 'nata' plus the maiden name), in Patrini, or in Conditio, and a question phrased 'did they live here?' names only one of those. (2) THE CONDITIO COLUMN IS SOCIALLY GRADED AND IS EVIDENCE IN ITS OWN RIGHT. It describes the GODPARENTS, not the child, and its values run rustici, villici, agricolae, supani (village headmen), judices, cives (townspeople), nobiles - often with a place attached, as in 'Cives Petinenses' or 'Rustici Lindarenses' or 'Nobiles Pisinenses'. For presence-or-absence questions that column is worth more than the names beside it: it tells you whether a person was of the town or visiting it, and the register withholds a place-epithet from people who are local. The same book's earlier narrative half, by contrast, labels outsiders freely ('Gollagoriciensis', 'Petinensis', 'ex Lindaro'), so a surname that is epithet-tagged before 1783 and bare after it has moved in. The ruled half also carries the parish's own copy of the 1788 Spiritual Visitation certificate at M01070195, and decanal sign-offs - 'Revisus in Visitatione Decanali die 7ma 8bris 1807, Petrus Anicich, Caes. Reg. Parochus et Decanus' at M01070225. The same dean signs the GOLOGORICA registers on 25 June 1808, so one decanal round covered both parishes and a single deanery protocol should account for them together. ALSO NOW OPENED on ZM34K-214, and it had never been read by anyone who recorded the fact: the GOLOGORICA MARRIAGE REGISTER 1770-1789, which sits inside the composite item at M01068953-M01069007 together with baptisms 1770-1781 and deaths 1770-1789 - three registers bound and filmed as one, with NO SIGNATURA on the Pazin paper inventory. The marriages occupy roughly M01068998-M01069006; the item's own KRAJ target is M01069007. Four things about this book are worth knowing before opening it, and the last two are the reason it is worth opening at all. (1) ENTRIES ARE NARRATIVE LATIN TO A FIXED FORMULA, one paragraph per marriage under a centred date heading, with the year carried only by an occasional centred divider rather than on each entry - so a frame can be read without the year being on it, and the year has to be taken from the nearest divider in either direction. (2) IT CARRIES A TRADE COLUMN INSIDE THE PROSE, as 'professionis suae [trade]' for the groom. The overwhelmingly common value is 'Agricola'; anything else on a page of Agricolae is a real statement about a man rather than a formula, and is worth magnifying before transcription because the short trade words differ by one letter (Textor, a weaver, against Tector, a plasterer). (3) IT NAMES THE PRIEST WHO OFFICIATED WITH HIS OFFICE AND HIS PARISH, in the ablative - 'a Reverendissimo Domino Archipresbytero et Parocho [place]ensi [name]' - and that priest is frequently NOT this parish's own. THIS IS THE TRANSFERABLE FINDING: a marriage register names the clergy of neighbouring parishes, so a priest whose own parish's surviving film begins too late to hold him may still be named, in full, in the register of a parish four kilometres away that was filmed from an earlier date. Anyone hunting an eighteenth-century Istrian parish priest should read the neighbours' marriage books before writing to a diocesan archive for a clergy list. (4) IT DISTINGUISHES SAME-NAMED MEN BY PATRONYMIC, as 'quondam [father] filius' for a dead father and 'filio Domini [father]' for a living one - which in a district where a handful of forenames repeat across every household is often the only thing in any register that tells two contemporaries apart. ONE UNSOLVED FEATURE, recorded so the next reader does not assume it: every entry carries a NUMBER IN THE LEFT MARGIN, and on a single opening these run 25, 110, 62, 102, 50, 6, 82, 27, 115, 45, 62, 34, 65 - out of order, with repeats, and too large to be ages. They are not sequential entry numbers and they have not been identified; do not read them as house numbers without testing it. Recurring surnames on the frames read so far: Udovicich, Chrismanich, Defranceschi, Millotich, Besiach, Zabran, Gasparich, Pascoli, Rabar, Bancich, Grah, Grabar, Sestan, Merklin, Rosa, Lucacich, Brosan. NO FAMILYSEARCH WAYPOINT EXISTS for this book either - like the Gracisce baptisms above it is a DAPA film read from a private copy of the reel, so it is recorded by frame range, not by waypoint. ONE MORE THING ON ZM34K-214, AND IT IS THE MOST USEFUL ITEM ON EITHER REEL FOR THE PRE-1784 GENERATION. The item the Pazin inventory files as 'Gologorica - Umrli - 1646-1806' (M01069199-M01069223) is NOT mainly a death register. It is a PERPETUAL OBIT CALENDAR, and it says so on its own title page at M01069202: 'Catalogus mortuorum in Parochia Gollogoritiae ADULTORUM, ab anno Christianae 1646 usque ad nostra tempora, ex antiquis et recentioribus paginis coactus a me Antonio Ferdinando Mocovrich, Parocho Loci, Anno Domini 1800.' Two months to an opening, the days of the month down each page, and against each day the people who died on that day IN ANY YEAR with the year ruled off at the right. In Italian, not Latin. It runs the full twelve months within about M01069202-M01069221 and was kept up by later hands long after 1806 - the same pages carry 1817, 1819, 1857 and 1887. WHY IT IS WORTH OPENING BEFORE THE REGISTERS. It is a digest, made in 1800, of parish registers running back to 1646 - and for a parish whose pre-1784 death books are not otherwise in the filmed set, it is the only surviving route to them. Sixteen openings read for one surname produced eleven dated entries spanning 1709 to 1804, several naming a filiation ('figlia q. [father]', 'moglie di q. [husband]'), a house number, an age, and occasionally a style such as Signor or Reverendo. For people who otherwise exist only as a year on a family tree it supplies the day, and often the household. THREE WARNINGS, ALL EARNED. (1) 'ADULTORUM' - IT EXCLUDES CHILDREN, so a nil in it is a nil for adults only and a family that buried only infants in the parish is invisible. (2) IT IS A COPY, NOT A WITNESS. For anything before 1800 it is derived from the registers, so where a later register also survives the two are not independent sources and must not be counted as corroboration of each other; what agreement shows is that the compiler copied accurately. (3) IT IS ORDERED BY DAY OF THE YEAR, NOT BY YEAR - you cannot turn to 1773, you must read all twelve months - and the YEAR COLUMN is the faint part of the page. In the entries read, names were crisp while years were blotted, cut at the gutter, or reduced to '170' plus an illegible stroke; every year has to be magnified against its neighbours on the same line, and a year must never be completed from a family tree you are trying to confirm. A first impression at page scale read one year as '177-' which at eight times proved to be '1751' - the difference between confirming a descent and not. Anyone working a central-Istrian parish should check whether its 'deaths' item is actually a book of this kind before planning a page-by-page walk. NOW READ END TO END ON ZM34K-214, and it is the clearest warning on either reel: the item the inventory files as 'Gologorica - Rodeni - 1764-1788', SIGNATURA 3.2, M01068915-M01068952, thirty-eight frames. Its shape is NOT one register. M01068915 is the film's printed title card, M01068916 a microfilm RESOLUTION TARGET and not a page at all, M01068917 the cover ('LIBER BAPTIZATORUM II.dus ... ab anno 1764'), M01068918-M01068941 the register running continuously from 1764 to May 1782, and M01068952 the film's KRAJ target. THEN THE TRAP. From 1782 the book SPLITS BY SEX into two sequences, each under its own centred heading: 'Masculi baptizati sub Parocho [name]' at M01068942-M01068947, and 'Foeminae baptizatae sub Parocho [name]' at M01068948-M01068951. A count taken from either run is a count of one sex, and a nil taken from one is a nil for half the parish. The same reel's DEATH register splits the same way, and this archive has already paid once for reading a split register as a whole one. SECOND, THE FIVE YEARS 1784-1788 ARE REGISTERED TWICE. This book runs to 21 September 1788 while the Gologorica baptism book 1784-1880 (M01069008 onward) opens in 1784, so the overlap is not a succession - the parish wrote the same baptisms into both volumes, and THE TWO COPIES DO NOT CARRY THE SAME FIELDS. For one child checked line against line, the later book supplied the house number, the midwife and a second forename while this one supplied the BIRTH DATE and the OFFICIANT, each omitting what the other had. Anyone working this parish for 1784-1788 who reads one volume has read half of every entry. THIRD, A DUPLICATE EXPOSURE HERE IS A DOCUMENT, NOT SPOILAGE. M01068929 and M01068930 are one opening photographed twice; on the first a LOOSE LEAF lies across both pages and obscures them, and on the second it has been lifted. The leaf is a certified word-for-word extract from a NEIGHBOURING PARISH'S baptism register, copied and signed by that parish's incumbent in 1793 and left inside this book ever since - so it names clergy of the next parish, at dates of its own, inside a volume catalogued under this one. That matches the three frame-pairs already recorded above for ZM34K-215: on these reels, re-shot openings are worth opening before they are written off as film debris. FOURTH, THE BOOK CHANGES ITS FIELDS TWICE AND A SWEEP DESIGNED ON THE EARLY FRAMES WILL NOT FIT THE LATE ONES. For seventeen years not one baptism carries a house number; from 8 November 1781, with a change of incumbent, EVERY entry carries one in the margin under a 'Domus Numerus' column, and from 1787 every entry also carries a PROFESSION for the father ('professione Agricola', 'Textor', 'Sator', 'Faber', 'Sutor'). The numbers run past 100, which is the same high range as the parish's own numbered house list of 1770 and not the compressed range of the 1826 census. FIFTH, A PATRONYMIC TRAP THAT IS NOT PECULIAR TO THIS PARISH. The village held, at the same time and both standing as godparents in this one book, two men of the SAME forename pair and the SAME patronymic differing only in surname - DEFRANCESCHI and DEPRATO, each written as 'Joannes Baptista ... Leonardi'. Where a surname is abbreviated, cropped, damaged or simply omitted, a patronymic names both men and distinguishes neither, and it feels as though it has done the work. SIXTH, THE VOLUME CARRIES EPISCOPAL VISITATION NOTES IN THE BISHOP'S OWN HAND, dated 15 July 1768 ('in prima Nostra Generali Visitatione, Revisus et approbatus') and 10 July 1775, which date the book's custody; the see is written 'Petinensis'. SEVENTH, THE REGISTER NARRATES ITS OWN CHANGE OF INCUMBENT, with a cause, in the entries themselves: through December 1781 and January 1782 a deputising priest records in the body of each entry that he is acting because the parish priest is ILL, naming him; the parish priest dies that month; and a month later the same hand has added 'et Parochus' to its own style. A handover that would otherwise have to be inferred from a gap between two books is written down inside one. Recurring surnames through the volume, for anyone deciding whether it is worth their time: Udovcich (often with the byname Gospod or Jacotich), Flegar, Crismanich, Zabran, Ancich, Gasparich, Deprato, Defranceschi, Sherbaz, Bancich, Marion, Crosgnich, Sestan, Rabar, Zaez, Pavelich, Selescho, Grah, Bobar (dictus Barron), Dujanich, Tencich, Uglessich. NO FAMILYSEARCH WAYPOINT EXISTS for this book either - a DAPA film read from a private copy of the reel, recorded by signatura and frame range. TWO MORE THINGS ABOUT THE DEATH HALF OF THE COMPOSITE ITEM ON ZM34K-214 (M01068975-M01068996), both found by reading it rather than scanning it, and both of a kind that will silently corrupt a count. (1) THE SEX SPLIT IS REAL BUT LEAKY. The men run M01068975-M01068987 and the women M01068988-M01068996, as the headings say - but each sequence carries the occasional stray of the other sex. A nil taken from one run is therefore not a nil even for that sex. (2) A DEATH CAN BE ENTERED TWICE. One burial of April 1783 appears in BOTH sequences, under the same house number and in the same hand, with the wording not identical between the two - one copy carries a clause the other omits and the burial day differs by a stroke. So the two runs cannot simply be added: the total double-counts, and where the two copies disagree neither is automatically the better witness. Together with the doubly-registered baptisms of 1784-1788 noted above, the working assumption for this parish should be that a single event may be written more than once in more than one book, and that the copies complement rather than confirm each other. THE DEATH ENTRIES THEMSELVES ARE UNUSUALLY FULL for the period: they commonly give the hour of death, the age in years, who administered the last sacraments and who performed the burial, each with office and parish - and the clergy named are frequently from OTHER parishes, so this book is also a source for the neighbouring clergy. From the mid-1780s they also give the place of burial as a choice between the old ground by the church and a 'novum Coemeterium extra locum', which dates the opening of a new burial ground. ONE MORE THING ABOUT THAT RULED HALF, and it is the complement of the warning above. The range M01070190-M01070226 (1784 to May 1808, about 800 baptisms) has now been read down EVERY column rather than one - Pater, Mater including its 'olim' and 'nata' maiden names, Patrini, Conditio and Baptizans. Two things that will cost the next reader time. (1) A LOOK-ALIKE SURNAME. In this hand the surname CINRICH reads convincingly as GRAH at page scale and does not survive magnification: the Cinrich initial is an open C with a long sweeping entry stroke, the Grah initial closes into a bowl. It was flagged as a hit twice and destroyed twice, and it recurs as a mother's 'olim' name on later frames. Any sweep of this book for a short surname has to magnify every candidate rather than trust the page. (2) ONE HOUSEHOLD IS WRITTEN UNDER TWO INITIALS. The same house number with the same two forenames appears as GRACH, as GRAH and once as PRACH; compared at one magnification against the same scribe's own P (Poldrugovaz) and G, the odd one is genuinely a P. So a surname index built from this book will split one family across two letters, and a search under one initial loses a fifth of the household's entries. Taken with the Pater/Patrini warning above, the working rule for this volume is that a surname can sit in any of four columns AND under more than one initial. The CONDITIO column repaid the full sweep: it graded one small household 'Cives' at all ten of its appearances across eleven years, and named the village SUPANUS and the JUDICISSA as godparents to its children, which is a social placement no name list would have given. THE FIRST ITEM ON ZM34K-214 IS NOT WHAT THE INVENTORY SAYS EITHER. The film's title card reads 'ZUPA: CEROVLJE · STATUS ANIMARUM · XIX-XX. ST. · SIGNATURA 3.2' and the frame map follows it, but the book's own cover label reads 'Status animarum CEROVLJE - PREVIZ' - two settlements, and Previz heads its own long run of pages. Four things make this a difficult 139 frames and are worth knowing first. (1) IT IS NOT ONE BOOK. Its page numbers run up to 292 and then start again at 1; the turn is visible on a single frame where the page carries '292' struck through and renumbered '2'. Any citation by page number is ambiguous unless it also says which sequence. (2) THERE IS NO INDEX. An apparently alphabetical run of surnames near the back is not one - it resumes non-alphabetical order on the facing page - so the book has to be read page by page. (3) THE FILMING SKIPS BLANK PAGES UNEVENLY: across the first sequence the page numbers advance about 3.1 per filmed frame, so roughly a third of its openings were never shot, while the second sequence advances about 1.9 and is nearly complete. A frame count is not a page count here. (4) THE PRINTED COLUMN HEADED 'Profectus in Religione' IS BEING USED FOR ORIGINS AND DESTINATIONS, not for religious progress: it carries entries like 'e Novaco', 'e Draguc', 'e Gologorica' and 'obiit Polae'. That makes it the direct equivalent of the 'Locus ex quo vel ad quem' column in the Gologorica 1826 census described above, and for anyone tracing movement into or out of central Istria it is the most useful column on the page. It has not been harvested. ONE MORE THING, AND IT SAVES A LETTER TO A DIOCESAN ARCHIVE: page 3 of this book carries 'Series curatorum in Cerovlje ab 9. novembris 1871' - a list of FIFTEEN incumbents from 1871 to 1979, each with the day he took the cure, the day he left it, and his tenure in years, months and days. Four of the fifteen are marked 'excurrendo', serving from another parish, and the list names which parish - three from Novaki and one from Gologorica, the latter for ten years from 1913. A parish census is not an obvious place to look for a clergy succession, and this one is better than most published lists. FINALLY, A SURNAME WARNING FROM THIS BOOK that applies to the whole district: one family appears under THREE forms of its name - the register's own ink form, a hyphenated compound with a byname attached, and an ITALIANISED form added in faint PENCIL above the household heading by a later hand. The pencil form is what an Italian-era index or civil record of the 1920s and 1930s would carry, and it is invisible to anyone searching the ink. Surname searches in Istrian parish books of this period should assume a Slavic form, a byname compound and an Italian form, and should look above the heading as well as in it. THAT CEROVLJE BOOK IS NOW READ END TO END, all 138 frames, and three further things about it are worth passing on. (1) THE SECOND SEQUENCE IS IN A DIFFERENT LANGUAGE. The first runs in Latin with Latin forenames; from the renumbering onward the same parish keeps the same printed form in CROATIAN - 'radnik', 'domacica', 'zemlj.' in the conditio column and Ivan, Marija, Andrija for Joannes, Maria, Andreas. A name index built from one half will not match the other, and the same household appears in both under two sets of forenames. (2) BECAUSE OF THAT DOUBLING, THE BOOK CHECKS ITS OWN HAND. One household's wife was read from the Latin half as a surname beginning in R; the Croatian entry for the same household, same husband, same birth date, writes it unmistakably with an F, and the F is right. Where a status animarum was recopied, read the copy before trusting a doubtful name in the original. (3) A LATER HAND ANNOTATED THE SLAVIC SURNAMES WITH THEIR ITALIAN FORMS IN PENCIL, above the household headings rather than in them, and in at least one place wrote the equation out - the Italian form, then 'ver.' for vero, then the Slavic form. That is the Italian-era name an index or civil record of the 1920s-30s would carry, and it is invisible to anyone searching the ink. A status animarum of this period in Istria should be searched under the Slavic form, any byname compound, AND the Italianised form. ONE MORE STRUCTURAL NOTE, because it has now happened three times on these two reels: a LOOSE DOCUMENT lying on an opening, photographed in place and then lifted for the next frame. The third instance is a certified extract from another parish's register, stamped and signed by that parish in 1959, lying inside a book catalogued under a different parish entirely. On DAPA film a repeated opening is a document until proved otherwise, and these inserts carry clergy names and dates from parishes the catalogue does not mention. TWO FINDING AIDS ON ZM34K-214 THAT ARE WORTH KNOWING BEFORE READING A PAGE OF IT. (1) THE GOLOGORICA BAPTISM BOOK 1784-1880 HAS AN ALPHABETICAL INDEX at its back, in the same household-directory form as the death book's described above: surname, byname, HOUSE NUMBER, then the household's children each with the PAGE of its baptism. It is about sixteen frames and it turns a 174-frame book into a lookup. Two cautions carry over from the death index and one is new. A married woman is filed under her HUSBAND'S surname, so the index is a directory of FATHERS and a name search of it will miss mothers and godparents entirely - a nil taken from it is a nil for households only. Letters with nobody in them are simply absent, so the sequence jumps (G straight to L in this parish), which is the book's own way of saying the shelf is empty rather than a gap in the filming. And the index itself carries the SAME DOUBLE HOUSE NUMBERING as the register: one household head is entered with a number struck through, a second written after it and a third beneath, so a number carried out of this index into another book needs to say which of the three it is. (2) THE 1826 STATUS ANIMARUM IS ONE TABLE ACROSS TWO PAGES and the surname column is on the LEFT half only; the right half carries marriage, death, the 'Locus ex quo vel ad quem' origins column and the annotations. A surname sweep therefore needs only the left halves, which makes a 121-frame book cheap to sweep - but anyone reporting a result from it should say which half they read, because the origins column is the valuable one and is not where the names are. The same book enters at least one household TWICE, pages apart, as the baptism books do for 1784-1788; and its tail records FOUNDLINGS TAKEN FROM TRIESTE into village households in 1844-1846, entered 'ex expositis Tergeste' with the date of assumption into nourishment - a route by which a child with no local parentage enters a rural parish's records under a surname that is not its own. THE OTHER THREE GOLOGORICA STATUS ANIMARUM ON ZM34K-214, and the most useful thing on this entry for anyone working Istria in the Italian period. (1) TWO OF THEM CARRY THEIR OWN FINDING AIDS. The 1894 book ends with a REPERTORIUM - an index keyed on surname-initial plus forename-initial, giving each person's HOUSE NUMBER and the PAGE of the census, with decade-banded age columns running 1800 to 1980. It indexes PEOPLE, not households, so it lists married women under their own surnames - which the baptism book's household index does not. Its main sequence is alphabetical; after it come supplement pages ('Dopunjak') in no order at all, so a surname search has to read those too. The 1862 book's index is a LOOSE PAPER SLIP laid across blank pages near the back, headed 'Ordo alfabeticus familiarum in hoc statu animarum contentarum'; it lists FAMILIES with their page, so a wife's maiden surname is outside it. Checking the back of these volumes before sweeping them turned 390 frames of work into about forty. (2) THE 1921 BOOK HAS NO INDEX, is damaged at the spine, and was kept up into the 1990s. (3) THE 1862 BOOK IS LAID OUT DIFFERENTLY FROM THE OTHERS: it carries a complete table on EACH page, where 1826, 1894 and 1921 run one table across the opening with the names on the left half only. A sweep designed on one will miss half of the other. (4) THE 1894 BOOK ALSO CARRIES A 'SENES' LIST - the parish's elderly as at 31 December 1908, ordered by birth date, each with house number and age to the year. For a parish whose older registers are patchy it supplies exact birth dates for people otherwise known only by a decade. (5) AND THE SINGLE MOST TRANSFERABLE THING: the 1921 book records, above a household heading, 'corretta in [Italian form], con decreto del prefetto di Pola' - CORRECTED BY DECREE OF THE PREFECT OF POLA. The Italianisation of Slavic surnames in Istrian parish books of the 1920s and 1930s was an administrative act, and the register sometimes names the authority. Combined with the pencil annotations described above for Cerovlje, the working rule for this period is: a surname search must try the Slavic form, any byname compound AND the Italian form, and must read the space ABOVE the household heading, because that is where the later hand wrote the imposed name and it is invisible to anyone reading the ink. (6) THE 1921 BOOK CITES THE DECREES THEMSELVES, AND THIS IS THE PART THAT CHANGES HOW YOU SEARCH. Read end to end 11 Oct 2026 (ZM34K-214, frames M01069826-M01069942, 117 of 117, 95 houses across some 25 hamlets), the annotations are not bare references to a decree but citations with DATE AND PROTOCOL NUMBER, written above the household heading: '= Opassi (D. Pref. 2/5-29 No 0-76)' over Opasic Franciscus at house 27, and '= Opassi (D. Pref. 4/5-29 No 0-80)' over Opasic Antonius at house 28 - separate decrees on consecutive days of May 1929, each with its own number. The annotations in this book run from 1929 to 1935. TWO CONSEQUENCES FOR ANYONE SEARCHING ISTRIAN RECORDS OF THIS PERIOD. (a) A MARRIED WOMAN'S MAIDEN NAME WAS DECREED SEPARATELY FROM HER HUSBAND'S SURNAME. At house 27 the wife is entered 'Aemilia ux. n. Ceh = Ceceo (D.Pr. 3/5-29 No 0-53)' - her birth surname changed in its own right, one day after his, under its own number. So the Slavic maiden name can be absent from a record in which the husband's Slavic name survives, and the reverse. (b) THE DECREED FORM NEED NOT SOUND LIKE THE NAME AT ALL. Three strategies appear in the one book: respelling by sound (Opasic>Opassi, Ceh>Ceceo, Braticic>Bratti, Androsic>Androssi, Silic>Silli, Sirol>Sirolli); clipping to an Italian shape (Ancic>Anci, Grzanic>Ghersani, Udovicic>Udovici, Rabar>Rabario); and OUTRIGHT TRANSLATION OF MEANING - 'Delle Vedove' is written over 'Udovicic Antonius' at house 70 under its own decree, Croatian udovica being a widow. The same surname went both ways in the same parish, clipped at one hamlet and translated at another. A phonetic search would never find the translated form, so the working rule is: try the Slavic form, the compound, the phonetic Italian form, the clipped Italian form, AND the Italian translation of what the name MEANS. (7) A RELATED TRAP IN THE SAME BOOKS: a hyphenated surname means one of two different things. Genuine two-family compounds are the standing convention of this parish (Rabar-Santelic, Zec-Kocebar, Zec-Jurandic, Rabar-Radetic), but the decrees produced an identical-looking hyphen that is ONE name written in both languages, Italian first - 'Rosa Opassi-Opacic', 'Regina Rabario-Rabar', 'Androssi-Androsic', 'Udovici-Udovicic'. Before reading a compound as two families, check whether the second element is simply the first one in Slavic. (8) A FILING NOTE FOR ANYONE HOLDING THESE REELS LOCALLY: the two folders split at M01069501, NOT at the reel boundary, so frames the frame map assigns to reel ZM34K-214 sit in the folder named ZM34K-215. Every frame is present; only the folder name misleads. (9) A PARISH INDEX CAN STOP LONG BEFORE ITS BOOK DOES, AND NOBODY LABELS THE POINT WHERE IT DOES. The Gologorica death register 1784-1880 (ZM34K-214, M01069226-M01069297) has an alphabetical index at the back (M01069299-M01069313) organised by household, which hands over house numbers, 'alias' bynames and an 'Extranei' column listing outsiders who died in the parish. It is genuinely useful and it is a trap: checked block by block, NOT ONE PAGE NUMBER ANYWHERE IN IT PASSES 71, while the register itself is written to page 135. Page 67 is 1826-27 and page 135 is January 1880, so the index covers the first forty-odd years of a ninety-six-year book and was then abandoned. A nil taken from this index is a nil to about 1830 and no further. The practical proof: the two death years this archive corrected by decades out of this book sit at pages 114 and 132, both outside the index, and neither could ever have been reached by consulting it. Before citing any parish index as a negative, find its highest page reference and compare it with the last written page of the book. (10) THE ITALIANISATION DECREES ARE NOT CONFINED TO THE STATUS ANIMARUM. The same '= [Italian form] (D.Pref. date No.)' annotation appears in the BAPTISM register: above the first entry of M01069131, over 'Antonius Opassich', '= Opassi: D.P. 15/VI-30 N.o 142' - Decreto Prefettizio, 15 June 1930, number 142. So a surname search of an Istrian baptism book for the 1920s-30s must also read the space ABOVE the line, not only the status animarum. (11) FOR A SURNAME THAT ONLY EVER MARRIED IN, THE GODPARENT AND MOTHER COLUMNS ARE THE WHOLE SEARCH, AND NO INDEX REACHES THEM. The Gologorica baptism book 1784-1880 has its own index, but like most it files a married woman under her husband's surname, so a wife's birth name is invisible to it. Reading the 'Nomen et Cognomen Parentum' and 'Nomen et Cognomen Patrinorum' columns of 99 frames (M01069037-M01069135, 1799-1860) produced exactly one instance of the surname sought, which the index could not have produced at all. Two practical notes for anyone doing the same: the column band SHIFTS between gatherings and the book changes format about 1829, so a fixed crop silently drops a column - re-check it frame by frame; and the Conditio Patrinorum column, which gives each godparent's parish, is where the real information often is, because it lets you read one entry against the clerk's own usage elsewhere on the page. (12) FOR A SURNAME THAT ONLY MARRIES IN, THE RECEIVING PARISH IS WHERE YOU FIND HER - AND IT IS THE RECEIVING PARISH THAT RECORDS WHERE SHE CAME FROM. A status animarum follows households, so a woman who marries out of a parish simply stops appearing in that parish's book and appears in her husband's. Worked example from ZM34K-214: the Cerovlje status animarum was swept end to end and gave the surname GRAH at houses 18, 19, 23, 38 and 53, with eight daughters marrying out into six named surnames. The Gologorica status animarum of 1862 (M01069464) then produced a Grah wife that book does not contain - 'Rosalia ux. n. Grah-Missan', born 13 May 1845, married 18 June 1869 - whose Adnotatio reads 'e Cerovglie N.o 12'. House 12 is not among Cerovlje's Grah houses and Bubic is not among the surnames its daughters married, because she left in 1869, before those households were drawn, and the numbering changed in between. The neighbouring parish's census therefore PRESERVES A HOUSEHOLD THE HOME PARISH'S OWN SURVIVING BOOK NO LONGER SHOWS. Sweep the neighbours' books, not only the home one, and read the Adnotatio column, which is where the origin is written. (13) A COMPOUND SURNAME MAY HAVE MORE THAN ONE SECOND ELEMENT, so matching on one compound silently misses the rest. The same reel gives both 'Grah-Missan' and 'GRAH-JOPAN' as wives' maiden names in a single opening. Search the bare surname and treat every compound as a separate term. (14) AND A CAUTION ABOUT SHORTCUTS ON SPARSE BOOKS: much of the 1862 Gologorica volume is blank, and the film carries its own 'BLANK PAGES / NEISPISANE STRANICE' target. An ink-density pass written to find the written pages and skip the empties classed M01069560 as blank; that frame carries about twenty-five names. On a printed, ruled census form the rules dominate the measurement and a sparsely written page scores like an empty one. Do not threshold these books - read every frame. (15) A STATUS ANIMARUM CAN BE A GENEALOGY RATHER THAN A HOUSE LIST, AND THE 1894 GOLOGORICA BOOK IS ONE. Swept end to end 11 Oct 2026 (ZM34K-214, register frames M01069580-M01069749). Under each household head it sets out named relationship blocks - 'Filii', 'Filiae', 'Fratres', 'Sorores', 'Parentes' - and, where the wife had married before, 'Liberi ... ex I thalamo' and 'ex II thalamo', HER CHILDREN BY EACH EARLIER HUSBAND, listed separately under the current one. That is rare and it is worth going out of your way for: it sorts a remarried person's children by marriage, which parish baptism registers almost never do, and it names siblings and parents of the head who may live elsewhere entirely. The 1862 volume of the same parish carries an equivalent recap section at M01069550-551. Do not treat a book of this class as a name list to be scanned - read the relationship headings. (16) AND THESE BOOKS CAN CARRY AN 'EXTREMA UNCTIO' REGISTER, WHICH IS A DEATH-ADJACENT SOURCE WHERE THE DEATH BOOK IS LOST. At M01069740 the 1894 Gologorica volume turns into a ruled register headed STATUS ANIMARUM whose columns are Nrus domus, NOMEN ET COGNOMEN, Pagus, Nativitatis (dies/mensis/annus), EXTREMA UNCTIO (dies/mensis/annus), Confessus, Communicans. It records last rites by year - 1907 eleven entries, 1908 ten, 1909 two - each person with a house, a hamlet and a FULL DATE OF BIRTH. Extreme unction is administered at the point of death. The Gologorica death register ends 23 January 1880 with 'Segue libro nuovo Vol. IV' and Vol. IV is on neither ZM34K reel, so for those three years this is the nearest thing to a death register that survives in reach. If a parish's death book is missing for a period, check the back of its status animarum for an unction register before concluding the period is unreachable. (17) THE 'SENES' LISTS ARE AN ANNUAL SERIES, NOT A ONE-OFF, AND A DISAPPEARANCE FROM ONE DATES A DEATH. The same book carries 'Annus 1899', 'Annus 1900', 'Annus 1901', 'Annus 1902', 'Annus 1903' and on, each headed with the preceding 31 December and each listing the parish's elderly with their ages. A single such list gives a birth date to the year; the SERIES gives something better, because the year a name stops appearing brackets the year of death. For a parish whose death register is missing this is a dating instrument, and it costs nothing once the book is open. (18) ALSO BOUND INTO THESE VOLUMES: NUMBERED SUCCESSION LISTS OF THE PARISH CLERGY. M01069737-39 gives thirty-one incumbents of Gologorica in order, from 'Trailizza Petinensis' to 'Curavic Joannes'. Three such lists have now been found across the two reels (also in the 1921 volume and in the Cerovlje book). They date an incumbency, which in turn dates a hand - useful when a register's entries are unsigned. (19) A METHOD WARNING FOR ANYONE TILING THESE FRAMES TO READ A SURNAME COLUMN. The ruled table SHIFTS position between gatherings, and these books change format mid-volume. A fixed crop that worked for fifty frames will silently clip the first letters of the surname column - in this sweep M01069612 came through as 'ubic' for 'Bubic'. For a surname search a lost initial hides exactly what is being looked for. Check the crop every few frames against the full page, and when it drifts, regenerate and RE-READ what was already read rather than carrying on.

providers.name: Državni arhiv u Rijeci
providers.what: The Rijeka State Archive — the Kvarner, Fiume's corpus separatum administration, and the Liburnian coast.

providers.name: Državni arhiv u Zadru
providers.what: The Zadar State Archive, which holds the Venetian and Austrian registers of Dalmatia — including parishes whose books never went to Split. Its own analytical inventory (HR-DAZD-378, ~2,400 civil-registry books) states the collection's scope explicitly: coastal Dalmatia from Rab in the north to Hvar and Vis in the south. Confirmed by walking the inventory's full parish list: it holds NOTHING for the inland Lika-Senj cluster (Sveti Rok, Lovinac, Gračac, Ričice, Donji Lapac, Gospić) — those parishes are out of scope for this archive, not merely unindexed. The site itself blocks automated/headless browsing (403) but loads normally in an ordinary browser. Its analytical inventory HR-DAZD-378 (Burić and Modrinić, 2014) is now held in data/dazd-378-registers.json: 178 parishes and 1,840 register books with the archive's own signatures, which is what a letter here has to quote.

providers.name: Bayerisches Staatsarchiv Nürnberg
providers.what: Nuremberg, under the Generaldirektion der Staatlichen Archive Bayerns. The state archives of Bavaria publish their holdings and say which services are free.
providers.triageNote: Surveyed 2026-10-09. gda.bayern.de opens with no account asked for; «kostenlos» appears in its own description of services.

providers.name: Bibliothek des Sächsischen Staatsarchivs, Standort Bergarchiv Freiberg
providers.what: The library of the Sächsisches Staatsarchiv at the BERGARCHIV FREIBERG — the mining archive of Saxony, and a reference library rather than a record office. Worth knowing for anyone whose people were miners in the Erzgebirge: the Bergarchiv holds the industry's own records. The library's catalogue is in K10plus, the shared German union catalogue.
providers.triageNote: Surveyed 2026-10-09. archiv.sachsen.de/bibliothek-8493.html opens with no account asked for and links opac.k10plus.de. This row is the library at the Bergarchiv Freiberg standort, not the record holdings themselves.

providers.name: Brandenburgisches Landeshauptarchiv
providers.what: Potsdam. The Brandenburgisches Landeshauptarchiv publishes its holdings and feeds them to Archivportal-D, the German federal archive portal, which is where a cross-state search for a Brandenburg holding should start.
providers.triageNote: Surveyed 2026-10-09. blha.brandenburg.de opens with no account asked for and links www.archivportal-d.de.

providers.name: Landesarchiv Berlin
providers.what: Landesarchiv Berlin. ITS NAME INDEXES ARE ONLINE AND FREE AND THE REGISTERS THEMSELVES ARE NOT. LABSA (the deep link) is a finding aid to the Namensverzeichnisse -- the name indexes to the birth, marriage and death registers of about 142 Berlin registry offices -- served as whole PDFs, no account, no fee, no viewer. Deaths run year by year to 1994, marriages stop at 1944 and births at 1913, because the protection period is 30 years for a death, 80 for a marriage and 110 for a birth. An index gives a surname, forenames, a day and month, a REGISTER NUMBER and often the confession; the register entry itself, with the address, age, birthplace and informant, is ordered from the archive for a fee. THE ORDERING COUNTER HAS ITS OWN ADDRESS AND IT IS NOT ON THE ARCHIVE'S SITE: copies, and the Sammelakten that sit alongside the marriage registers, are ordered through the Digitaler Antrag at service.berlin.de/dienstleistung/352800/. TWO DEFECTS MEASURED IN USE. The search form's three record-type checkboxes DO NOT UNION -- ticking more than one corrupts the result (Schoeneberg returns 61 death volumes alone and 0 with all three ticked), so query one record type per request. And the office name must be exact, with the 'Standesamt ' prefix, double-encoded for the 29 offices whose names carry an umlaut or eszett. ALSO: the PDFs are labelled 'Durchsuchbares PDF durch OCR-Texterkennung' and that label is not a promise about the NAMES -- where a volume is handwritten the OCR has caught the printed headings and almost nothing else, so a volume's text layer must be scored against common surnames before its silence is allowed to mean anything. MEASURED FURTHER, 11 OCTOBER 2026, ACROSS 45 CONSECUTIVE VOLUMES OF ONE OFFICE'S DEATH INDEXES. (1) THE TEXT LAYER BEGINS IN A PARTICULAR YEAR AND THAT YEAR MUST BE FOUND, NOT GUESSED: in this office it begins at 1963, the series changing from a handwritten index to a typed one, and the file size drops from about 125 MB to about 33 MB with it. A prediction made from one blind volume and its legible neighbour was wrong by seventeen volumes. Score every volume. (2) THE MARRIAGE INDEXES ARE EFFECTIVELY IMAGE-ONLY: all 313 volumes to 1944, 28.3 GB, score zero control names a page. They are free to download and cannot be searched by machine at all. The 209 birth-index volumes to 1913 are the same. Anyone planning a marriage search here is planning to read, not to grep. (3) THE BOROUGH REGISTRY OFFICES DID NOT EXIST BEFORE 1938. A pre-1938 Berlin birth or marriage is under Standesamt Berlin I to XIII, or Rixdorf, or Charlottenburg I to IV, and searching the modern borough names for those years finds nothing because there is nothing to find. (4) INDIVIDUAL VOLUMES ARE DEFECTIVE IN WAYS THAT INVALIDATE A BRACKET SEARCH: some are not alphabetical within a letter but run by month and date, some are scanned mirrored on every page, some hold several alphabets in one volume, and some have their pages out of sequence. Where any of these is true the whole letter must be read. (5) The letter blocks sit at stable fractions of the way through the volumes of a given office and era, so the band can be rendered in one go rather than hunted. (6) WHAT THE THREE INDEX KINDS ACTUALLY GIVE YOU, measured on Charlottenburg I and II. A BIRTH INDEX gives the child's surname and forenames, the day and month, and THE REGISTER NUMBER — and nothing else; it does not name the parents, and the “Zugehörigkeit zu einer Kirche” column is routinely blank. It locates a certificate, it does not replace one. A MARRIAGE INDEX IS WORSE: IT GIVES SURNAMES ONLY, no forenames, and NO INDICATION OF WHICH PARTY IS THE GROOM. A widow remarrying appears under her own married surname with “geb.” and her new husband opposite, so a man of surname X marrying a woman of surname Y and a woman of X marrying a man of Y look identical on the page. AN INDEX HIT NAMES A MARRIAGE, NOT A COUPLE. Birth indexes are arranged BY LETTER THEN BY MONTH; marriage indexes BY LETTER THEN BY YEAR. (7) AND THE ORDER THAT MAKES ANY OF THIS AFFORDABLE: DIRECTORY FIRST, THEN OFFICE, THEN INDEX. Berlin had well over a hundred registry offices and a surname sweep across them is hopeless; a street directory for the right year names the household, gives the street, and the street fixes the office. One volume instead of seventeen. (8) THE TEXT LAYER BEGINS IN A DIFFERENT YEAR IN EVERY OFFICE AND THE BOUNDARY IS SHARP, SO MEASURE IT PER OFFICE AND NEVER CARRY IT OVER. Three measured so far: KREUZBERG's death indexes begin reading at 1963, SCHÖNEBERG's at 1984, and EVERY EAST BERLIN OFFICE's at 1991 — all ELEVEN 1990 volumes — which is every registry office in East Berlin — score 0.000 while the 1991 volumes of the same offices score 1.4 to 2.5. There is nothing in between: a series is either 0.00-0.03 or above 1.3. And one office can defy its neighbours — Prenzlauer Berg is blind through 1993 while the other ten read from 1991. (9) WHETHER A MARRIED WOMAN IS CROSS-INDEXED UNDER BOTH HER NAMES IS AN OFFICE'S HABIT, NOT A RULE. Köpenick files her twice, once under each (“Leibner” and “Wilk geb. Leibner”, same register number); Spandau filed one woman once, under her birth name, with her married surname only as the second element of the line. SO A READER WHO READS ONLY ONE LETTER BLOCK — which is what a blind volume forces — WILL MISS A WOMAN THE REGISTRAR DID NOT CROSS-INDEX. A band reading is a narrower negative than a whole-volume one and should be written down as one.

providers.name: Landeskirchliches Archiv Braunschweig
providers.what: Landeskirchliches Archiv Braunschweig — a German state or church archive. German civil registration began in 1876 and parish registers before it are largely with the Landeskirchliche Archive, so which of the two holds a record depends on its date. Harvested from Wikidata and its address opened; what is online and what it costs is unchecked.

The Protestant church books of Bavaria are not free: this archive is a member of ARCHION, the Kirchenbuchportal, a paid subscription, and that is where its digitised registers are. In July 2026 the NÜRNBERGER KIRCHENBUCHVERKARTUNGEN — the card indexes to the Nuremberg registers, which are the shortcut through them — went online there too. The archive itself gives free advice and runs online transcription classes for the handwriting.

providers.name: FamilySearch
providers.what: The largest free collection of record images and indexes in the world. A free account is required, and a minority of images are restricted to Family History Centres and affiliate libraries. TWO TRAPS IN THE CROATIAN HOLDINGS, both verified by use on 2026-10-09 and both capable of producing a confident false nil. (1) THE SAME PARISH SITS IN MORE THAN ONE COLLECTION. Bakar (Buccari) records are indexed under BOTH 'Croatia, Church Books, 1516-1994' (cc=2040054) AND 'Croatia, Delnice Deanery Catholic Church Books, 1571-1926'. A search restricted to 2040054 returns ZERO for records that demonstrably exist in the Delnice Deanery set - a marriage of 1783 at Bakar was found only once the collection filter was dropped. So a nil reported against one Croatian collection is a statement about that collection, never about the parish; and the catalogue's film list for a place may be split across collections that do not cross-reference each other. (2) SEARCH URL PARAMETERS SILENTLY FAIL. Hand-built query strings of the form /search/record/results?q.surname=X&q.anyPlace=Y returned 'Historical Record Search Results (0)' for a record whose own detail page gives exactly that surname and exactly that place string. The same query typed into the search form returns it. Place and collection parameters are the ones observed to fail; a bare q.surname + q.givenName pair did work. THE PRACTICAL RULE: never report a FamilySearch nil from a URL you assembled. Drive the form, and run a known-positive control - an ark id you already hold - through the same path first. An index entry is also a pointer and not a reading: the 1783 marriage above is indexed as two names and a date, and the words 'ex Gollogorizza' in the entry itself - the words that place the groom 130 km away in another crown land and make the record foreign to the Bakar set it sits in - appear nowhere in the index. Open the image before building or dismissing a household on an indexed record. Film and image-group identifiers DO work as stable handles where this collection's viewer carries no wc= waypoint: the Bakar marriage volume is film 005494714, 'Bakar. Religious Marriage Registers 1739-1808', item 1, 226 images, image group M99F-VRM. FULL-RESOLUTION IMAGES CAN BE DOWNLOADED, and it is worth knowing because the viewer's own zoom is a poor substitute for cropping locally. The download control in the image viewer opens a dialog offering 'PDF Record Image with Highlights', 'PDF with No Highlights', 'JPG Only' and 'No Record Image'. Choose JPG Only: it delivers the plate at native scan resolution - a Croatian parish register leaf came down at 5975x4206 - named <filmnumber>_<imagenumber>.jpeg, e.g. 005494714_00172.jpeg, which is a self-describing filename worth keeping. Note that the DeepZoom tiles the viewer itself loads (service/records/storage/deepzoomcloud/dz/v1/apid:<APID>/image_files/<level>/<col>_<row>.jpg) return 401 to an unauthenticated fetch and are blocked by CORS from the www origin, so scraping them is neither possible nor necessary; the download button is the supported route and it works. Resolution matters for more than comfort: a contested initial letter in a surname was settled only by cropping two words at identical magnification from the downloaded file, and the same comparison attempted through the viewer's zoom had been inconclusive.
